'''Liu Gang''' (Chinese: 刘刚; born 30 January 1961) is a Chinese-born American aerospace engineer, computer scientist, optical physicist, political activist, and writer. He founded the [[Beijing Students' Autonomous Federation]]. He was a prominent student leader at the [[Tiananmen Square protests of 1989]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Tiananmen's Most Wanted |url=http://sinosphere.blogs.nytimes.com/2014/06/03/tiananmens-most-wanted/ |author=Andrew Jacobs |date=June 3, 2014|work= [[The New York Times]]|access-date=June 3, 2014}}</ref> Liu holds an M.A. in physics from [[Peking University]] and an M.A. in [[computer science]] from [[Columbia University]]. After his exile to the United States in 1996, Liu studied technology and physics at [[Bell Labs]] in [[New Jersey]]. Liu was employed at [[Morgan Stanley]] as a [[Wall Street]] IT analyst.<ref>{{cite web |title=From China's Prisons To Columbia's Computers |url=http://engineering.columbia.edu/web/newsletterarchive/archive/engnews_s98/liu.html |publisher=Columbia University |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100612000554/http://engineering.columbia.edu/web/newsletterarchive/archive/engnews_s98/liu.html |archive-date=June 12, 2010|access-date=July 10, 2016}}</ref>

== Student activist ==
As an undergraduate student at [[University of Science and Technology of China]] in [[Hefei]], Liu met [[Fang Lizhi]], a pro-democracy activist.<ref>{{cite web |title=Guilt by Association: More Documents from the Chinese Trials. News from Asia Watch. P.2 |url=https://www.hrw.org/legacy/campaigns/china/scholars/t15/China0791.PDF |date=July 25, 1991 |publisher= News from Asia Watch |access-date=July 10, 2016}}</ref> Then, at [[Peking University]], Liu organized "Democracy Salons". [[Wang Dan (dissident)|Wang Dan]] later held a position there.

Liu was a 28-year-old graduate when the 1989 demonstrations began. He organized the [[Beijing Students' Autonomous Federation]] and joined the movement's organizing body. As a result, he was sixth on a list of twenty-one activists whose arrests were ordered by the government. Liu went into hiding as a fugitive, but on 15 June 1989, Liu was arrested and charged with attempted subversion of the [[Chinese Communist Party]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/06/21/world/china-arrests-another-student-leader.html?action=click&module=Search&region=searchResults&mabReward=relbias%3As&url=http%3A%2F%2Fquery.nytimes.com%2Fsearch%2Fsitesearch%2F%23%2FLIU%2BGANG%2F |title=China Arrests Another Student Leader |author=Nicholas D. Kristof |date=June 3, 2014 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=July 10, 2016 }}</ref> In 1991, he was convicted and sentenced to six years imprisonment at [[Qincheng Prison]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Democracy Leader on Trial in China |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/01/24/world/democracy-leader-on-trial-in-china.html |author=Sheryl WuDunn |date=January 24, 1991 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=July 10, 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=China Tries Another Student for Protests |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/02/07/world/china-tries-another-student-for-protests.html\ |author=Sheryl WuDunn|date=February 7, 1991|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=July 10, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Imprisoned China Pro-Democrats Charge Torture |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/09/01/world/imprisoned-china-pro-democrats-charge-torture.html?action=click&module=Search&region=searchResults&mabReward=relbias%3As&url=http%3A%2F%2Fquery.nytimes.com%2Fsearch%2Fsitesearch%2F%23%2FLIU%2BGANG%2F |author=Nicholas D. Kristof |date=September 1, 1992 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=July 10, 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=A Gentler China: A special report.; 4 Years After Tiananmen, The Hard Line is Cracking |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/06/01/world/gentler-china-special-report-4-years-after-tiananmen-hard-line-cracking.html?gwh=2237D3A723BEAC4F49BC8D04C4402AC7&gwt=pay |author=Nicholas D. Kristof |date=June 1, 1993 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=July 10, 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Chinese Government Shows Video Of 4 Prisoners Mentioned by U.S. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/03/02/world/chinese-government-shows-video-of-4-prisoners-mentioned-by-us.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=2 March 1994 |access-date=July 10, 2016 |last1=Tyler |first1=Patrick E. }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Chinese Said to Detain Dissidents as Parley Nears |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/08/10/world/chinese-said-to-detain-dissidents-as-parley-nears.html?action=click&module=Search&region=searchResults&mabReward=relbias%3As&url=http%3A%2F%2Fquery.nytimes.com%2Fsearch%2Fsitesearch%2F%23%2FLIU%2BGANG%2F |date=August 10, 1995 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=July 10, 2016 }}</ref>

After his release from prison in 1996, Liu continued to advocate for [[human rights in China]] and organized an underground democracy movement.<ref>{{cite web |title=Chinese Take Journalists on Guided Tour of Prison |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/03/06/world/chinese-take-journalists-on-guided-tour-of-prison.html |author=Patrick E. Tyler |date=March 6, 1994 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=July 10, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=World News Briefs; China Releases Dissident After 6 Years in Prison |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/06/19/world/world-news-briefs-china-releases-dissident-after-6-years-in-prison.html |date=June 19, 1995 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=July 10, 2016 }}</ref> After moving to the United States, Liu continued his studies at Columbia University in New York City.<ref>{{cite web |title=A Top Dissident Flees China And Is Admitted to the U.S. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/05/04/world/a-top-dissident-flees-china-and-is-admitted-to-the-us.html/ |author=Steven Erlanger |date=May 4, 1996 |work=[[The New York Times]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110216070927/http://www.nytimes.com/1996/05/04/world/a-top-dissident-flees-china-and-is-admitted-to-the-us.html |archive-date=February 16, 2011 |access-date=July 10, 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Chinese Exiles Wonder How Wind Will Blow |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/02/21/world/chinese-exiles-wonder-how-wind-will-blow.html?gwh=4C58AA6327BC321F009EF33CB7A9FC6C&gwt=pay |author=Richard Bernstein |date=February 21, 1997 |work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=July 10, 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Liu Gang |url=https://concernedscientists.org/1997/10/liu-gang/ |date=October 3, 1997 |publisher=Committee of Concerned Scientists |access-date=July 10, 2016 }}</ref> From there, he continued to support the Chinese democracy movement and in 2011, initiated further [[2011 Chinese pro-democracy protests|pro-democracy protests]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Torment of Tiananmen |url=https://nypost.com/2011/08/07/torment-of-tiananmen/ |author=Kathianne Boniello |date=August 7, 2011 |publisher=[[New York Post]]|access-date=August 7, 2011}}</ref>

== Scientific research ==

=== China ===
In 1982, Liu received a bachelor's degree in modern mechanics from the [[University of Science and Technology of China]]. He was employed by the [[Aviation Industry Corporation of China]] in [[Shenyang]] in the field of [[aerodynamics]]. He worked in partnership with [[Luo Yang (aircraft designer)|Luo Yang]], and was promoted to head of [[aircraft design process|aircraft design]]. Liu's field of research was the theory of [[air resistance]], and he worked on problems of double-sided entry and [[radar]] technology.

In 1984, Liu received a master's degree in [[optics]] from the Department of Physics at [[Peking University]] in [[Beijing]]. While there, he was an assistant teacher.<ref>{{cite web|title=Introduce of the China's 21 "Most Wanted" following Tiananmen Square Massacre|url=http://chinadailymail.com/2013/06/13/chinas-21-most-wanted-following-tiananmen-square-massacre/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130622144734/http://chinadailymail.com/2013/06/13/chinas-21-most-wanted-following-tiananmen-square-massacre/|url-status=usurped|archive-date=June 22, 2013|date=June 13, 2013|publisher=China Daily Mail|access-date=June 13, 2013}}</ref> Liu returned to work at the China Soft Science Research Institute but was also acting assistant director at the University of Science and Technology of China.

In 1988, Liu became an assistant and associate researcher at the Wear-Resistant Materials Development Company of the National Ministry of Higher Education and the [[Dalian Institute of Technology]].{{citation needed|date=April 2015}} He was then transferred to research in the Department of Physics at the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]].

=== United States ===
In 1996, Liu received a master's degree in computer science from Columbia University. He was invited to speak at the [[New York Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Wang Dan Press Conference Statement|url=http://www.hrichina.org/en/content/2773|date=April 23, 1998|publisher=Human Rights in China|access-date=July 10, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230131232154/https://www.hrichina.org/en/content/2773|archive-date=January 31, 2023|url-status=dead}}</ref> Liu gained employment as a member of technical staff (MTS) at the Mathematics of Networks and Systems Research Department at Bell Laboratories in [[Murray Hill, New Jersey|Murray Hill]], New Jersey. There he worked on [[Optical telecommunication]] network design and planning, [[routing]] [[algorithms]], [[optimization]] techniques, and [[economic model]]s and [[strategy]] analysis.<ref>{{cite web|title=Introduce of Gang Liu|url=http://cm.bell-labs.com/cm/ms/who/gang/index.html|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140806081009/http://cm.bell-labs.com/cm/ms/who/gang/index.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 6, 2014|publisher=Bell's Lab|access-date=July 10, 2016 }}</ref>

Liu's areas of research included: SPIDER, a design tool for fast-restoration in all-optical networks; VPNStar, a system for provisioning multi-service [[VPNs]] with [[Quality of service]] guarantees over [[Internet Protocol]]; in software design, a management system for Lambda Router in all-optical networks; and analysis of [[Internet]] pricing.<ref>{{cite web|title=Active Research Projects of Gang Liu|url=http://cm.bell-labs.com/who/gang/proj.html|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140806081005/http://cm.bell-labs.com/who/gang/proj.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=2014-08-06|publisher=Bell's Lab}}</ref>

During his days at Bell Laboratories, Liu introduced the A*Prune (1999, {{ISSN|0743-166X}}) with K. G. Ramakrishnan, to describe a new class of [[algorithm]]. This opened a new research direction in [[theoretical science]]. He found that A*Prune is comparable to the current best known-approximate algorithms for most randomly generated [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]]. The algorithm constructs paths, starting at the source and going towards the destination. But, at each iteration, the [[algorithm]] is rid of all paths that are guaranteed to violate the constraints, thereby keeping only those partial paths that have the potential to be turned into feasible paths, from which the [[optimal]] paths are drawn.<ref>{{cite web|title=A*Prune: An Algorithm for Finding K Shortest Paths Subject to Multiple Constraints|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/2370289|date=August 2001|publisher=Research Gate|access-date=July 10, 2016}}</ref>

Liu also proposed a special class of Optical devices called SPIDER (2001, {{ISSN|1089-7089}}); optical routers, dense [[wavelength division multiplexing]] (DWDM) systems, and cross-connects of unprecedented capacities. Liu and his colleagues are developing techniques for efficient and reliable [[Optical telecommunication|optical network]] design, covering decentralized dedicated protection to shared path-based mesh restoration.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Davis|first1=R. Drew|last2=Kumar|first2=K.|last3=Liu|first3=Gang|last4=Sanlee|first4=Iraj|title=SPIDER: A Simple and Flexible Tool for Design and Provisioning of Protected Lightpaths in Optical Networks|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220440646|publisher=Research Gate|date=March 2000|access-date=11 July 2016}}</ref>
